steps.intent: Our primary objective is to secure a straightforward, 12-month extension of the mandate of the 1718 Committee Panel of Experts to ensure uninterrupted, independent, and objective monitoring of UN sanctions violations and North Korea's prohibited weapons programmes. The most significant difficulty will stem from the Russian Federation and China, who are demanding structural changes to the sanctions regime, including sunset clauses on the measures and restrictions on the Panel's investigation of illicit military and arms-transfer cooperation between Pyongyang and Moscow. Preserving the integrity and independence of the Panel's mandate without conceding to sunset clauses or sanctions rollbacks remains our red line, despite the acute risk of a Russian veto.

China.change: Decides to conduct a comprehensive review of the sanctions measures imposed by relevant resolutions with a view to introducing a sunset clause, and to consider adjusting, suspending, or lifting relevant measures in light of the humanitarian situation and developments on the Korean Peninsula.

Insert after PP8: 'Reiterating that the measures imposed by relevant resolutions are not intended to have adverse humanitarian consequences for the civilian population of the DPRK or negatively affect humanitarian assistance, and underscoring the necessity of assessing and mitigating the humanitarian impact of sanctions,'

Replace with: 'Underscores that the Panel shall carry out credible, fact-based, independent, and strictly objective assessments, analysis, and recommendations in accordance with the mandate of the Panel of Experts as specified in paragraph 26 of resolution 1874 (2009), while avoiding politicization and unsubstantiated allegations;'

Russian Federation.change: Decides to conduct a comprehensive review of the sanctions regime against the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea and to establish a 12-month sunset clause on all restrictive measures imposed by previous resolutions, with the measures expiring unless extended by a decision of the Security Council.
replace '30 April 2025' with '30 October 2024' and replace '28 March 2025' with '28 September 2024'

add at the end: 'and calls upon the Panel to thoroughly assess and report on the negative humanitarian consequences and unintended economic impacts of Council sanctions on the civilian population of the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea;'

messages.Algeria: Algeria supports the proposed draft resolution extending the mandate of the Panel of Experts assisting the 1718 Committee. Maintaining an objective, fact-based, and independent mechanism to monitor the implementation of Council resolutions is essential for the global non-proliferation architecture. We also emphasize the necessity of pursuing genuine diplomatic engagement and de-escalation to achieve lasting peace and stability on the Korean Peninsula.
messages.China: China has consistently maintained that Security Council sanctions against the DPRK cannot be indefinite or set in stone, and must not exacerbate the humanitarian hardships faced by the DPRK population. We support incorporating a sunset clause and regular review mechanism to ensure the sanctions regime serves a political settlement rather than collective punishment. We urge the penholder to accommodate these constructive and legitimate concerns to maintain unity within the Council.
messages.Ecuador: Ecuador fully supports the draft resolution renewing the mandate of the Panel of Experts assisting the 1718 Sanctions Committee. The Panel's independent, objective, and fact-based reporting is essential for monitoring the implementation of Council sanctions and supporting our shared non-proliferation objectives. We favor the adoption of the text as drafted without weakening its core mandate.
messages.France: France fully supports the draft resolution extending the mandate of the Panel of Experts assisting the 1718 Committee for another year. The Panel's independent, objective, and fact-based reporting is vital to maintaining the integrity of the international non-proliferation architecture and tracking the DPRK's continuous sanctions evasion and unlawful weapons development. We urge all Council members to preserve the Panel's mandate intact and adopt the text without weakening or politicizing its essential monitoring role.
messages.Guyana: Guyana supports the draft resolution extending the mandate of the 1718 Panel of Experts as circulated. The Panel's objective, fact-based reporting remains essential for monitoring the implementation of Council measures and supporting our collective non-proliferation commitments. We favor a straightforward, technical renewal of the mandate to ensure the continuity of the Panel's vital work.
messages.Japan: Japan fully supports the draft resolution extending the mandate of the 1718 Committee Panel of Experts for another year. In the face of the DPRK's continued and unprecedented ballistic missile launches and advancing nuclear weapons programmes, the Panel's independent, objective, and fact-based monitoring is more critical than ever. We commend the United States for preparing this timely draft and call on all Council members to adopt the text without weakening the Panel's essential role.
messages.Malta: Malta fully supports the draft resolution as presented by the United States to extend the mandate of the 1718 Panel of Experts for another year. The Panel's objective, independent, and fact-based reporting is essential for assisting the Council and member states in implementing sanctions and addressing the serious proliferation risks posed by the DPRK. We see no need for substantive changes and favor a clean and timely adoption.
messages.Mozambique: Mozambique supports the draft resolution extending the mandate of the Panel of Experts assisting the 1718 Committee, as technical and objective monitoring remains vital for upholding the global non-proliferation architecture. We value the Panel's independent, fact-based reporting and believe its continued work assists Member States in fulfilling their obligations. At the same time, we urge all Council members to maintain unity and foster constructive dialogue aimed at de-escalation and a peaceful, diplomatic solution on the Korean Peninsula.
messages.Republic of Korea: The Republic of Korea fully supports the draft resolution renewing the mandate of the 1718 Panel of Experts for another year as circulated. The Panel's independent, objective, and fact-based reporting remains indispensable for monitoring the implementation of Council sanctions amid the DPRK's continued ballistic missile and nuclear activities and widespread sanctions evasion. We thank the United States for its leadership as penholder and urge all Council members to support the text without weakening or diluting the Panel's mandate.
messages.Russian Federation: The open-ended, suffocating sanctions regime against the DPRK is completely detached from reality and serves solely to punish ordinary citizens and exacerbate tensions on the Korean Peninsula. The Council cannot continue auto-renewing the Panel of Experts as a politicized instrument for Western interests while ignoring the need for a sunset clause and comprehensive review of these outdated measures. Unless a clear sunset clause and review mechanism for the sanctions regime are incorporated into this draft, the Russian Federation will not be able to support it.
messages.Sierra Leone: Sierra Leone supports the draft resolution renewing the mandate of the Panel of Experts assisting the 1718 Sanctions Committee. Independent, objective, and credible reporting is vital to supporting the Council's non-proliferation objectives and maintaining international peace and security. We encourage all Council members to constructively support this routine technical extension.
messages.Slovenia: Slovenia fully supports the draft resolution as presented by the penholder to extend the mandate of the 1718 Panel of Experts for another year. The Panel's independent, objective, and fact-based reporting is vital for monitoring sanctions implementation and upholding the global non-proliferation architecture. We favor a clean renewal and stand ready to vote in favor of the text as drafted.
messages.Switzerland: Switzerland fully supports the draft resolution as presented by the United States to extend the mandate of the 1718 Panel of Experts for another year. The independent, fact-based reporting and analysis of the Panel remain essential for monitoring sanctions implementation and supporting the work of the Council amidst the DPRK's continuing nuclear and ballistic missile programmes. We also appreciate the continued reflection of resolution 2664 (2022) to safeguard humanitarian assistance.
messages.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: The United Kingdom fully supports the draft resolution circulated by the United States to extend the mandate of the 1718 Committee Panel of Experts for another year. The Panel's independent, fact-based reporting remains essential for monitoring the implementation of Security Council sanctions as the DPRK continues to advance its unlawful weapons programmes. We urge all Council members to support this straightforward, standard renewal text without diluting or undermining the Panel's vital mandate.

steps.summary: As penholder, the United States maintains a clean, straightforward 12-month extension of the 1718 Committee Panel of Experts' mandate, firmly supported by an overwhelming majority of Council members. The United States rejects Russian and Chinese demands to introduce sunset clauses or truncate the Panel's mandate, which would severely compromise the global non-proliferation architecture and silence critical reporting on illicit weapons proliferation and sanctions evasion. The text is put to a vote in its current form to defend the integrity and independence of UN sanctions monitoring.

before.Russian Federation:
Mr. President,

The Russian Federation will vote against the draft resolution submitted by the United States on the extension of the mandate of the Panel of Experts of the Committee established pursuant to resolution 1718 (2006).

For years, the Security Council's sanctions against the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea have remained completely detached from reality on the ground. Indefinite, open-ended sanctions regimes have proven incapable of resolving the security concerns of the Korean Peninsula or facilitating political and diplomatic dialogue. Instead, these measures have become an instrument of economic strangulation, imposing an unacceptable humanitarian burden on the population of the DPRK while doing nothing to deter military posturing and aggressive escalation by the United States and its regional allies.

The Panel of Experts, rather than fulfilling its mandate to provide independent, objective, and fact-based analysis, has increasingly degenerated into a tool servicing the geopolitical interests of Western capitals, relying on biased methodology and dubious media reports. 

During the consultations on the draft resolution, Russia made a constructive and pragmatic proposal to establish an objective review mechanism and introduce a sunset clause for the sanctions regime, so that the Security Council could regularly assess whether these measures remain relevant or need adjustment. Regrettably, the penholder and its Western allies flatly rejected our constructive compromise, demonstrating their complete lack of interest in adapting the sanctions architecture or pursuing genuine dialogue. Under these circumstances, continuing the work of the Panel of Experts in its current politicized format is utterly unjustified.

after.China:
(spoke in Chinese): The current situation on the Korean peninsula continues to be tense, with confrontation and antagonism on the rise. That serves the interests of no one and is the last thing China wants to see. The Korean peninsula issue is complicated and intractable, with a long history. It is, in essence, a security issue. The fundamental way to break the deadlock and resolve the issue is to build mutual trust, abandon the obsession with sanctions and pressure, and resume dialogue and consultations.

Sanctions are a means, not an end. Security Council sanctions against the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea should be implemented in a comprehensive, accurate, and balanced manner, without having a negative humanitarian impact on the livelihood of its people. Indefinite and open-ended sanctions cannot solve the problem; rather, they only exacerbate tensions. In the face of the ongoing deadlock on the peninsula, the Security Council should play a constructive role, facilitate the easing of tensions, and create conditions for political dialogue, rather than merely relying on sanctions.

China has always participated constructively in the consultations on the draft resolution submitted by the United States. During the consultations, we, together with Russia and other Council members, put forward reasonable and constructive proposals, including establishing a sunset mechanism for the sanctions regime and addressing the humanitarian situation, with a view to breaking the current stalemate and finding a peaceful settlement. Regrettably, those legitimate concerns and constructive proposals were not accepted, and the penholder insisted on pushing the draft resolution to a vote while major differences still remained, thereby compelling Council members to take positions and deepening divisions within the Council. In that context, China had no choice but to abstain in the voting on the draft resolution.

China’s position on the issue of the Korean peninsula is clear and consistent. We remain committed to maintaining peace and stability on the peninsula, achieving its denuclearization, and resolving the issue through dialogue and consultations. We will continue to actively promote peace talks, uphold the dual-track approach and the principle of phased and synchronized actions, and play a constructive role in working with all parties to achieve the long-term peace and stability of the peninsula and the region.
after.France:
(spoke in French):

France deeply deplores the veto cast today by the Russian Federation, which puts an end to the mandate of the Panel of Experts assisting the 1718 Committee. 

For 14 years, the Panel has carried out independent, objective, and vital work to monitor the implementation of sanctions unanimously adopted by this Council against the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea. By ending its mandate, Russia has chosen to blind the Security Council and the international community to the flagrant violations of the non-proliferation regime.

There should be no doubt about the motives behind this veto: Russia is seeking to prevent the Panel from reporting on its own growing violations of Security Council resolutions, specifically its procurement of arms and ballistic missiles from North Korea to fuel its war of aggression against Ukraine. By shielding Pyongyang from scrutiny, Russia has struck a severe blow to the global non-proliferation architecture and compromised the credibility and authority of the Security Council.

France reminds all States that the sanctions regime established by this Council against the DPRK remains fully in force. All Member States have an obligation under the Charter of the United Nations to strictly implement these resolutions. France remains fully committed to the complete, verifiable, and irreversible denuclearization of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea and will continue to work tirelessly with its partners to uphold international peace and security.

I thank you.
after.Japan:
Japan deeply regrets that the draft resolution before us today was not adopted due to the negative vote of a single permanent member, the Russian Federation.

For nearly fifteen years, the Panel of Experts has played a vital and indispensable role in assisting the Security Council and the 1718 Committee by providing credible, objective, and fact-based reporting on the implementation of and non-compliance with the Council’s sanctions against North Korea. The Panel’s independent work has been essential for all Member States to uphold the non-proliferation regime and to implement the resolutions unanimously adopted by this Council.

Today, 13 members of the Council voted in favour of extending the mandate of the Panel of Experts. Yet, Russia chose to silence this independent and objective reporting mechanism. Russia’s irresponsible use of the veto today seriously undermines the Council’s credibility, weakens the global non-proliferation architecture, and serves only to shield its own unlawful arms transactions with North Korea in direct violation of multiple Security Council resolutions. This self-serving veto is completely unacceptable.

We must be clear: today’s vote does not in any way alter the legal status of the sanctions measures imposed by this Council. All Security Council resolutions concerning North Korea, and the obligations of all Member States to implement them fully and faithfully, remain fully in force. 

North Korea continues to advance its unlawful nuclear and ballistic missile programmes at an unprecedented pace, threatening the peace and security of Japan, the region, and the entire international community. Japan once again urges North Korea to comply with all relevant Security Council resolutions, to immediately cease all provocative actions, and to abandon all nuclear weapons, existing nuclear programmes, and any other weapons of mass destruction and ballistic missile programmes in a complete, verifiable, and irreversible manner. We also urge North Korea to immediately resolve the abductions issue, which is a matter of utmost importance and urgency for Japan.

Despite this deeply regrettable outcome, Japan remains steadfastly committed to working with Council members and the wider international community to ensure the full implementation of the relevant Security Council resolutions and to uphold the international non-proliferation regime.

I thank you, Mr. President.
after.Republic of Korea:
Mr. President,

The Republic of Korea deeply regrets that the draft resolution before us today, which sought to extend the mandate of the Panel of Experts assisting the 1718 Sanctions Committee, was not adopted due to the veto cast by the Russian Federation, despite the overwhelming support of 13 Council members.

For the past 15 years, the Panel of Experts has served as a cornerstone of the Council’s efforts to uphold international non-proliferation and ensure the implementation of resolutions concerning the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK). Through its independent, credible, and fact-based reporting, the Panel has shed light on the DPRK’s relentless advancement of its unlawful nuclear and ballistic missile programs, as well as its sophisticated sanctions-evasion techniques.

Until today, the mandate of this Panel had been renewed annually by consensus, reflecting the Council’s shared conviction that proliferation of weapons of mass destruction and their delivery systems by the DPRK poses a grave threat to international peace and security. 

Today’s veto, however, is a clear abdication of the responsibilities of a permanent member of the Security Council. Russia’s action today is nothing less than destroying a CCTV camera to avoid being caught red-handed. It is an attempt to silence an independent reporting mechanism precisely because the Panel began uncovering evidence of illicit military cooperation and arms transfers between the DPRK and the Russian Federation, in flagrant violation of multiple Security Council resolutions that Russia itself voted in favour of.

Let us be unequivocally clear: while the mandate of the Panel of Experts may end, all existing Security Council resolutions and the sanctions measures imposed on the DPRK remain fully in place and legally binding on all Member States under Chapter VII of the United Nations Charter. The Council’s 1718 Committee continues its work, and the obligation of every Member State to strictly implement the sanctions remains unchanged.

The Republic of Korea will continue to work closely with the international community to faithfully implement all relevant Security Council resolutions, monitor illicit activities, and maintain our unwavering commitment to the complete, verifiable, and irreversible denuclearization of the DPRK.

Thank you, Mr. President.
after.Slovenia:
Mr. President,

Slovenia voted in favour of the draft resolution extending the mandate of the Panel of Experts assisting the 1718 Committee, and we deeply regret that, due to the veto cast by a permanent member, the Council was unable to adopt it today.

For nearly fifteen years, the Panel of Experts has provided the Security Council, the Sanctions Committee, and the wider United Nations membership with independent, objective, and fact-based reporting and analysis regarding the implementation of Council resolutions on the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea. Its work has been an indispensable tool in monitoring compliance and tracking proliferation networks and sanctions evasion.

The termination of the Panel's mandate comes at a critical juncture, as the DPRK continues its unlawful development of nuclear weapons and ballistic missile programmes in blatant disregard and violation of numerous Security Council resolutions, thereby threatening regional and international peace and security. Dismantling this vital monitoring mechanism severely undermines the Council's credibility and weakens the global non-proliferation regime.

Slovenia reiterates that the sanctions regime established by this Council remains fully in force. All Member States are legally bound under the Charter of the United Nations to fully and effectively implement all relevant Security Council resolutions. We urge the DPRK to immediately cease all destabilizing actions, abandon its weapons of mass destruction and ballistic missile programmes in a complete, verifiable, and irreversible manner, and return to dialogue.

Thank you.
after.Switzerland:
Switzerland deeply regrets that the Security Council was unable to adopt the resolution extending the mandate of the Panel of Experts assisting the 1718 Sanctions Committee due to the veto cast by the Russian Federation. 

For 15 years, the Panel of Experts has played a vital role in providing independent, objective, and fact-based reporting on the implementation of the sanctions regime. Its assessments and recommendations are an indispensable source of information not only for the Committee, but for all Member States striving to fulfill their obligations under the relevant Council resolutions. The termination of the Panel’s mandate weakens the Council’s non-proliferation architecture and deprives the international community of critical insight into illicit procurement networks and sanction-evasion activities at a time when the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea continues to accelerate its unlawful nuclear and ballistic missile programmes.

Switzerland voted in favour of the draft resolution because we firmly support the non-proliferation regime and the integrity of Council-mandated expert mechanisms. We thank the United States, as penholder, for its transparent and constructive efforts throughout the negotiations to reach a compromise. 

We wish to underline that, despite today’s outcome regarding the Panel of Experts, the Security Council sanctions measures against the DPRK remain fully in force and legally binding on all Member States, in accordance with the Charter of the United Nations. All States remain obliged to strictly implement these resolutions.

Switzerland remains committed to the goal of the complete, verifiable, and irreversible denuclearization of the Korean Peninsula and calls on the DPRK to respect its international obligations, cease its provocative actions, and return to meaningful dialogue.
after.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort:
Mr President,

The United Kingdom is deeply disappointed by the outcome of today’s vote. We voted in favour of this resolution to renew the mandate of the 1718 Panel of Experts, as 13 members of this Council did today, because the Panel’s independent, objective and fact-based reporting is essential to monitoring the implementation of Council sanctions and supporting global non-proliferation.

Russia’s veto today is reckless, irresponsible and deeply damaging. It does not reflect genuine concern for the humanitarian situation in the DPRK, nor for the effectiveness of the sanctions regime. Rather, it is a blatant attempt by a permanent member of this Council to silence independent scrutiny of its own violations of Security Council resolutions. 

Over recent months, we have seen Russia procure weapons and ballistic missiles from the DPRK for use in its illegal war of aggression against Ukraine, in direct and egregious violation of multiple resolutions that Russia itself voted to adopt. Russia is using its veto to shield itself from scrutiny and to bury reports on its own illicit arms transfers.

This veto strikes a severe blow to the global non-proliferation regime and undermines the credibility of the Security Council. It emboldens the DPRK to advance its unlawful weapons of mass destruction and ballistic missile programmes with impunity, threatening regional and international peace and security.

Let me be entirely clear: today’s veto terminates the mandate of the Panel of Experts, but it does not alter the fact that the sanctions against the DPRK remain in full force. All Member States remain bound by their obligations under relevant Security Council resolutions to fully implement these measures. 

The United Kingdom will continue to work closely with our partners to counter the DPRK’s proliferation activities, expose sanctions evasion networks, and uphold the integrity of the international non-proliferation architecture.

Thank you, Mr President.
after.United States of America:
Today, Russia used its veto to silence the independent 1718 Committee Panel of Experts, a body that has operated for 14 years with the unanimous support of this Council. Today’s vote is nothing more than the cynical effort of one permanent member to silence objective, independent reporting on its own ongoing violations of Security Council resolutions.

For over a decade, the Panel of Experts has been the gold standard for independent, fact-based reporting on the DPRK’s unlawful weapons of mass destruction and ballistic missile programs, as well as sanctions evasion efforts. Every single member of this Council has previously recognized the value of the Panel’s credible and impartial reporting. Yet today, Russia cast a veto because the Panel began reporting in recent months on Russia’s blatant violations of the DPRK sanctions regime—specifically, its procurement of DPRK ballistic missiles and munitions to fuel its illegal, unprovoked war of aggression against Ukraine. 

Russia’s actions today have jeopardized international peace and security to advance a corrupt bargain with Pyongyang. Russia attempted to hold the Panel hostage by demanding sunset clauses and arbitrary timelines for dismantling the sanctions regime itself—demands that had nothing to do with the Panel’s mandate and that ignored the DPRK’s reckless, ongoing proliferation and unprecedented missile launches.

Let me be absolutely clear: today’s veto does not dismantle the DPRK sanctions regime. The substantive measures imposed by the Security Council in resolutions 1718, 1874, 2270, 2321, 2371, 2375, and 2397 remain fully in place. All UN Member States remain legally obligated under Chapter VII of the UN Charter to comply with and enforce these sanctions. Russia’s veto cannot erase those obligations, nor can it hide the reality of its unlawful arms transfers with the DPRK.

The United States, alongside the overwhelming majority of this Council and the international community, remains firmly committed to countering the threat posed by the DPRK’s unlawful WMD and ballistic missile programs. We will continue to work with our allies and partners to pursue transparency, accountability, and the full implementation of Security Council resolutions. We once again call on the DPRK to abandon its dangerous, destabilizing path and return to meaningful dialogue without preconditions.
